title: TCL’s AI home begins with the TV
summary: TCL’s Inspiration Habitat at IFA 2026 is designed to look like a home rather than a conventional technology booth. The company placed its televisions, appliances and other devices in living spaces,…

blocks.text: TCL’s Inspiration Habitat at IFA 2026 is designed to look like a home rather than a conventional technology booth. The company placed its televisions, appliances and other devices in living spaces, giving visitors an idea of how they might actually fit together outside an exhibition hall.

The TV will always be front and center for the TCL brand but TCL has built much of its reputation around displays, and the X11L SQD-Mini LED TV is a good example of why the category remains central to the company. Its large screen immediately draws attention, while the rest of the room puts it into context alongside the other technology TCL wants to bring into the home.

The X11L is the flagship of TCL’s latest SQD-Mini LED lineup. TCL says the technology is designed to deliver more precise control over brightness and contrast while maintaining a wide color range and high HDR performance.

Other displays filled out the range. The C8L SQD-Mini LED TV received an IFA Innovation Award Honoree recognition, while the X3 Series OLED+ Gaming Monitor was recognized for its contrast, refresh rates and design. TCL also had its P80 Series smartphones on display, extending the company’s focus on screens into mobile devices.

The RayNeo products took that idea further. The RayNeo iO Smart Glasses incorporate an AI assistant, while the RayNeo GT Max AR Glasses combine augmented reality with Dolby Vision. TCL received an IFA Innovation Award Honoree recognition and a Global Product Technology Innovation Award for the GT Max, which the company describes as the world’s first Dolby Vision-certified AR experience.

The displays were the easiest part of TCL’s strategy to appreciate because the company has spent so much time refining this category. What became more interesting as I went through the showcase was seeing how that same emphasis on technology was being applied to less glamorous parts of the house.
The washing machine was a good example.

TCL’s AI SuperDrum Laundry Tower P9 Ultra initially struck me as a feature I did not really need. Washing machines have been doing their basic job for a long time, and it is not difficult to select a cycle for a normal load of laundry. Adding artificial intelligence to the process can sound like another example of a manufacturer finding a place to put AI simply because AI is now expected in consumer electronics.

The machine uses Generative AI Wash to assess the laundry and adjust the washing process. Instead of requiring the user to determine which cycle is appropriate for every load, the machine is designed to make that decision itself.

That is a small convenience, but it is also the sort of thing that makes more sense the longer you think about it. Laundry involves a series of repetitive decisions that people generally do not want to spend much time making. If the machine can reliably handle some of those decisions, then the AI has a straightforward and clear purpose.

The feature was a useful reminder that AI does not necessarily have to produce something spectacular to be useful. In this case, its job is simply to reduce the amount of attention required from the person doing the laundry.

TCL is applying similar ideas to other appliances. Its FreshIN 3.0 Ultra Air Conditioner uses AI to adjust its operation, while its refrigerator lineup incorporates intelligent functions intended to make food storage more convenient. The company is also adding AI capabilities to its 5G AI CPE X5 Router, which received an IFA Innovation Award Honoree recognition for its agentic features.

These products were presented alongside TCL’s NXTHOME concept, which combines connected appliances and displays with the design of the home itself. The approach makes sense of the large number of products on display because they are not presented simply as individual devices. TCL is trying to show what happens when those devices become part of the same environment.
The most unusual addition but adorable to the showcase is the AiMe, TCL’s Family Companion Robot.

AiMe is also the easiest product in the showcase to find endearing. It is a small robot designed to interact with people through multimodal capabilities and physical movement, with TCL positioning it as a companion that can support children and assist parents with everyday routines.

Unlike the appliances, AiMe does not disappear into the background once it starts working. Its physical presence is part of the product. That makes it a very different interpretation of an AI-powered home, and it gives the concept something that the more practical appliances do not have.

It is easy to imagine why a visitor would spend more time looking at AiMe than at a washing machine. The robot is visually interesting and deliberately designed to interact with people. The washing machine, by comparison, is successful precisely when it lets you forget about it.

Both approaches appeared throughout TCL’s showcase. Some of its AI features are designed to automate decisions that would otherwise be made by the user, while products such as AiMe are intended to create a new form of interaction inside the home.

It remains a device that people actively use, but TCL is increasingly surrounding it with technology that can respond to the environment and the people using it. The company’s Screen Universe concept reflects that broader approach, extending its display technology from large televisions to monitors, smartphones and AR glasses.

Walking through the Inspiration Habitat gave me a better sense of TCL’s direction than looking at any of its products on their own. The X11L is impressive as a television, but seeing it surrounded by appliances, mobile devices, networking equipment and AI-powered systems makes it easier to understand where TCL is taking its technology. The company is no longer treating the television as an endpoint. It is using the display as the starting point for a much larger ecosystem, with the rest of the home gradually becoming part of the same connected experience. the room.
